note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Young woman with 2 days of gradually worsening suprapubic (just below the umbilicus) burning abdominal pain, subjective feverishness and pink-discoloured urine — working impression: acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) being treated empirically.

History:
- Presenting complaint and timeline:
  - Lower central abdominal/suprapubic burning pain for ~2 days; gradual onset, fairly constant, worsening; sore to pressure.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - Mild nausea, feeling hot/sweaty (subjective feverishness).
  - Noted pink-coloured urine; increased urinary frequency (patient attributes some of this to high fluid intake).
  - No dysuria reported (no stinging/burning when passing urine).
  - No vomiting. Bowel movements currently normal (recent constipation last week that has improved).
  - No cough, shortness of breath, palpitations, headache, or visual symptoms reported.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No objective temperature recorded.
  - No vomiting, no diarrhea, no reported vaginal bleeding or abnormal vaginal discharge.
- Past medical history, allergies, medications:
  - Generally fit and well; no prior surgeries.
  - Contraception: Implanon implanted ~1 year ago.
  - No other regular medications reported.
  - No allergies mentioned in the transcript.
- Social / preventive health factors:
  - Sexually active with a single partner; last sexual activity 4 days ago.
  - Last STI screen normal ~6 months ago.
  - Last menstrual period ~2 weeks ago.
  - Lives in a shared house; works as an accountant.
  - Non-smoker; social alcohol use.

Examination:
- Vitals: none documented.
- Physical / observed findings:
  - Suprapubic tenderness reported on palpation by clinician ("sore when I press on it").
  - Patient subjectively felt hot and sweaty.
- No other physical exam details (no flank tenderness, no pelvic exam) documented.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression:
  - 1) Acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) — most likely.
    - Supporting evidence: focal suprapubic burning pain and tenderness, new urinary frequency, pink-discoloured urine (possible hematuria), mild nausea and subjective feverishness; clinician elected empirical antibiotic therapy.
  - 2) Urolithiasis (distal ureteric or bladder stone) — moderate likelihood.
    - Supporting/opposing: pink urine and lower abdominal pain could reflect hematuria from a stone; pain described as constant burning (less typical colicky pattern) and no flank-to-groin radiation, which argues against classic ureteric stone.
  - 3) Gynecologic causes (ectopic pregnancy, ruptured ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion) — moderate likelihood.
    - Supporting/opposing: lower pelvic pain and possible bleeding are compatible; however Implanon reduces pregnancy risk, no vaginal bleeding or unilateral severe adnexal pain reported, and no hemodynamic instability.
- Note on DDx consistency:
  - DDx ranking is consistent with the transcript; it guided listing of alternative possibilities but did not provide new conflicting facts.

Plan:
- Treatment given / recommended in consult:
  - Empiric antibiotic prescribed: Trimethoprim to be started today. Verbal dosing given in the consult was inconsistent (see Quality checks) — patient instructed to collect script at pharmacy and start antibiotics.
  - Analgesia: Paracetamol advised as needed for pain.
  - Supportive measures: maintain adequate oral fluids; cranberry juice suggested for urinary symptoms.
- Tests and follow-up:
  - Tests discussed: urine testing (urinalysis/culture) and pregnancy test; clinician offered to organize tests but patient elected to start antibiotics first. Clinician emphasized the importance of performing a pregnancy test.
  - Safety-netting and follow-up: return or contact clinician if symptoms worsen or do not improve in a few days; seek urgent care for worsening abdominal pain, persistent high fever, vomiting, or other concerning signs.
- Additional recommendations from DDx consistent with transcript:
  - Consider urine analysis/culture if symptoms persist or to confirm diagnosis.
  - Consider pregnancy testing to exclude pregnancy-related causes (ectopic pregnancy) given ongoing lower abdominal pain despite Implanon.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vital signs (temperature, pulse, blood pressure).
  - Results of any urine dipstick/urinalysis or urine culture (none performed/documented).
  - Pregnancy test result (not done / not documented).
  - Details of a pelvic/vaginal exam or speculum/ bimanual exam (not performed/documented).
  - Imaging if stone or gynecologic pathology suspected (not ordered/documented).
  - Explicit documentation of allergies.
  - Precise antibiotic dosing and duration in unambiguous terms (see conflicts).
- Conflicts noted:
  - Antibiotic dosing ambiguity: clinician’s spoken instructions included both "two tablets" and "one tablet twice a day for three days" — transcript is internally inconsistent about exact number/strength of tablets. (This is a transcript ambiguity rather than a DDx conflict.)
  - No other substantive conflicts identified between the transcript and the DDx summary; DDx expanded differential reasoning consistent with transcript findings.
- Transcript quality assessment:
  - Overall adequate and coherent for history-taking; includes key symptoms and clinician counselling.
  - Ambiguities: antibiotic dosing instruction unclear; no vitals or physical/pelvic exam details recorded; it is not explicit whether urine testing was ultimately arranged.
